extracted.intended_audience: student journalists, college campus community, and general readers interested in journalism ethics
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion piece reflecting on the Janet Cooke fabrication scandal and arguing for ethical standards in journalism, aimed especially at student and early-career journalists. It uses the historical case to draw lessons about credibility, accountability, and professional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "This business is built on one word: credibility. Journalists have a responsibility to the people which is to deliver the truth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility is fundamental: reporting must be truthful because fabrication undermines readers' trust and the profession as a whole. The Cooke case shows how a single fabricated story makes readers skeptical of what exactly is the truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fabrication / Truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: "It should always be done the right way. The truthful way where there’s no fabrication in sight, only the facts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not invent or embellish facts or sources. Stories must be based on verifiable facts and firsthand reporting rather than created details; fabrication is an ethical breach with severe consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and ownership of mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooke "should have taken accountability for her actions and not have blamed the success of Woodward and Bernstein".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When errors or misconduct occur, journalists should accept responsibility rather than deflect blame. Blaming others for personal ethical failures is an anti-pattern; transparency and correction are the ethical response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real sources / interview actual subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: "She could have helped children who were actually addicted to drugs. There were children who she could have interviewed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should seek and rely on real people and verifiable sources rather than fabricating characters or scenes. Doing so can bring attention and help to actual victims rather than imaginary ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do no harm / consider impact on vulnerable populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabricated reporting "made readers skeptical" and caused "the children who actually needed the help" to be forgotten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists must consider how reporting affects vulnerable communities; false stories can divert attention and resources away from real needs and stigmatize entire groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional consequences and career risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooke's fabrication led to returning the Pulitzer and long-term career fallout (now working as a sales clerk; "that ship has sailed").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication can destroy reputations and careers. Reporters should weigh short-term recognition against potentially irreversible professional consequences of ethical breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of bias and extra scrutiny faced by minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: "Cooke’s decision to fabricate the story ... left a stigma on African-American journalists ... future employers may associate me with her. Will they scrutinize my work more than my peers?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that ethical failures by individuals from marginalized groups can produce disproportionate stigma; journalists from such groups may need to anticipate greater scrutiny and work proactively to demonstrate credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper motivation: emulate truthful role models, not fame
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooke blamed the success of famous reporters; the author argues to "use them as motivation to deliver the best news story possible, without fabrication."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspire to the standards of respected, truthful journalists rather than copying the pursuit of fame. Integrity should drive reporting, not the desire for awards or notoriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist pressure for sensationalism / manage desire for recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: As a student journalist the author notes the pressure to make stories the best possible and to receive praise, but insists on doing it "the right way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should resist pressure to sensationalize or fabricate in order to win praise. Ethical reporting requires prioritizing accuracy and fairness over accolades.
